    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Can you fix a scratched CD? Here are your options

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You can try toothpaste or wax, but do so at your own risk.
    • Industry observers note that just like vinyl records before them, CDs are back.
    • The first step to fixing a CD that's skipping or not playing is to see if it just needs to be cleaned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You can try toothpaste or wax, but do so at your own risk.

    Industry observers note that just like vinyl records before them, CDs are back. As strange as it may seem if you grew up with them, CDs have become a nostalgic icon of the joys of physical media — but they're also a reminder of why we all went digital in the first place. The biggest drawback of CDs was always just how easy it can be to ruin one with a careless scratch, and that hasn't changed. If you're embracing CDs for the first time or taking them for a spin again because of the CD revival, a scratch may seem like the end for your favorite album, but there are a few time-tested ways to get your discs back in playing shape.

    The first step to fixing a CD that's skipping or not playing is to see if it just needs to be cleaned. Oils from your hands and debris like dust can cause playback complications without actually damaging the disc and they're easy enough to wipe away. To start, grab a lint-free cloth like microfiber and use it to wipe the CD from the center to the outer edge. Don't wipe across the CD, as this can cause more damage. For really dirty discs, you can use a little 70 percent isopropyl alcohol or distilled water applied to the cloth, though this typically isn't necessary. If you use any kind of liquid, make sure it's completely dried before you try to play or store your discs.

    For deeper scratches, there are a few time-tested DIY methods you'll find recommended often, but none of them are foolproof. Keep in mind that if you're taking disc repair into your own hands, there's no guarantee that you'll actually make things better, and there's some chance you'll make the problem worse. That being noted, it's entirely possible to buff out scratches and make CDs playable again, but whether it works depends on just how bad the damage is in the first place. For DIY disc repair, the goal is to use some form of abrasive to sand down the layer of the CD with a scratch, letting the player's laser reach the data stored deeper in the disc.

    According to recent reports, toothpaste is one of the most common cleaners to use, since it's cheap, accessible and not too damaging. Make sure you have plain white toothpaste without any gels, beads or whitening agents, and squirt a bit on the disc. Spread it evenly, then use a lint-free cloth to wipe from the inside of the disc outward a few times, all around the disc. Then rinse it off with water and let it dry. You can perform the same process with a stronger abrasive like 3M rubbing compound if you prefer.

    Industry observers note that if your disc still doesn't work, you can apply a thin layer of wax (like shoe polish or Chapstick) to seal the scratches. Just apply the wax from the inside of the disc to the outside and wipe it away using the same motion after a few minutes. Remember to let any product you apply dry completely before using your disc.

    In a recent development, for scratches you can't get out yourself, disc repair services are also an option, though they're rare these days and you may not have one near you. These services use professional-grade machines that essentially buff discs the same way that home methods do, but they can be more reliable. If you're really serious about preserving your discs, you can also buy one of these high-end machines yourself, but since they can run into the thousands of dollars, it's not an option for most people. In most cases, seeking professional repair or buying a disc repair machine only makes sense if you're trying to preserve rare CDs with material you can't find elsewhere.

    Recent findings suggest that if you want to preserve the data on your CD and you're not precious about the disc itself, it's a good idea to invest in a CD burner. This lets you copy the data on the disc, keeping it safe even if the physical CD is damaged. Making copies is a good idea, since your CD collection won't last forever. In some cases, a burner may be able to record the data from a disc even when scratches are causing it to skip in your CD player, letting you make another copy later. Like with any repair method, the success of a CD burner depends on how damaged the disc is, but it's a non-destructive way of preserving your CD's contents when it works.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Amazon fights Delivery Protection Act by putting stickers on its packages

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (466 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Amazon is placing a sticker on some of its delivery boxes to urge customers to oppose a New York City bill.
    • This weekend, some Amazon shoppers reported getting a delivery from Amazon with a sticker on it that reads: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.
    • Amazon is looking to stoke opposition to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Amazon is placing a sticker on some of its delivery boxes to urge customers to oppose a New York City bill.

    This weekend, some Amazon shoppers reported getting a delivery from Amazon with a sticker on it that reads: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The sticker reportedly includes a QR code that leads to a link for contacting NYC Councilmembers. The sticker encourages the package’s recipient to “Scan to tell your council member: no increases for Fresh Yorkers.”.

    Amazon is looking to stoke opposition to Introduction 0518-2026 (518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. The proposed law would require Amazon and other companies with last-mile delivery facilities in the city, such as FedEx, to directly employ third-party contractors Amazon uses for making deliveries.

    Amazon previously sent mailers to NYC residents regarding a new headquarters (which was subsequently scrapped), but political messaging on packages is unprecedented for Amazon, which hasn’t used its delivery boxes to lobby for political causes before.

    Last week, Amazon made another uncharacteristic move by showing NYC shoppers a homepage banner ad—which I see when logging in to Amazon as of this writing—and an in-app pop-up that also urges opposition to the bill. The banner and pop-up include a link to a blog where Amazon says the law would force it to consider moving operations outside of NYC and lead to “slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.” Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, however, support the bill.

    By using its packages, website, and app to advocate against the bill, Amazon hopes to leverage its large customer base to push a political ideal. This raises concerns about whether it’s presenting the debate fairly, the appropriateness of using an e-commerce platform for political purposes, and whether we’ll see more political messaging while shopping with Amazon or other companies in the future.

    As it stands, some shoppers are already put off by Amazon’s lobbying.

    “Something about this just feels off to me,” a Reddit user who apparently received a package with the sticker wrote.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sheikh Hasina has been living in exile in India since 2024.

    Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has mentioned she aims to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.

    Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson noted.

    The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.

    It has been revealed that but it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule. She denies the charges.

    Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.

    "Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.

    Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.

    Sources indicate that india's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ârequest for comment. In April, âthe ministry mentioned it was â examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the newly introduced government and further strengthen bilateral ties".

    Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.

    What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.

    On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.

    "Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he stated in a statement.

    Recent findings suggest that the choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.

    Sources indicate that abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.

    Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.

    The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.

    The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.

    But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.

    Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.

    "I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.

    Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.

    India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a fresh government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.

    According to recent reports, but nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.

    Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.

    The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

    President Trump praised Nvidia’s decision on Monday to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, saying on his social network Truth Social that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”.

    The Nvidia board’s statement had also referred to consultations with “senior levels of the United States government” as informing its decision. It stated that, based on that input, Mr. Huang’s reinstatement was deemed not a national security risk.

    Recent findings suggest that in his comments on Monday, Trump claimed that U.S. Attorney General [Todd Blanche] had found no evidence that Mr. Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct. It’s an unusual statement for a U.S. president to make, as the attorney general typically conducts those investigations independently. Notably, Attorney General Blanche has not yet made a formal statement on the case.

    Industry observers note that there’s also indication that President Trump may have been aware of the decision before the announcement by the Nvidia board. Speaking to a PBS journalist over the weekend, he remarked of Huang “he’s back where he should be and we see he did absolutely nothing wrong.” Asked to clarify about whether he meant Huang would be reinstated, Trump said, “I hope so, I hope so.”.

    Huang was accused of having multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a direct report at Nvidia and another unnamed employee. However, the affair of most concern was the one with the alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation). Ms. Huang was an executive at a Singapore-based organization called Megaspeed, which had purchased billions in Nvidia chips over the past couple of years. This relationship had raised national security concerns about whether the CEO ties to Ms. Huang could have compromised sensitive information or facilitated China’s access to advanced U.S. AI chips, which are subject to export restrictions.

    Industry observers note that trump remarked last week that he believed this relationship didn’t threaten the U.S.’s national security, and instead said that no one had proven she’s a spy. “She may not be a spy,” the president said, adding that “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”.

    Trump’s full statement on Huang’s return, released on Monday, is below.

    The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.

    EU imposes import quotas for hybrid vehicles from China

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The European Union confirmed on Tuesday that it was capping the number of hybrid vehicles that can be imported into the bloc from China.
    • The quota is to stand at around 15% on top of the volume imported in the previous year.
    • The announcement follows an agreement made between the EU's trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Trade Minister Wang Wentao in October.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The European Union confirmed on Tuesday that it was capping the number of hybrid vehicles that can be imported into the bloc from China.

    The quota is to stand at around 15% on top of the volume imported in the previous year.

    The announcement follows an agreement made between the EU's trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Trade Minister Wang Wentao in October.

    China, on Tuesday, called on the EU to stick to the "compliant, and balanced" agreement the two sides had reached.

    The cap is set to come into effect on December 1.

    "These restrictions are needed to protect EU industry against a sharp recent increase in imports of such vehicles … [following] an investigation that showed imports of hybrid vehicles into the EU have increased significantly since 2023," the European Commission noted in a statement.

    "The surge in imports of hybrid passenger vehicles into the EU has been driven by growing global production overcapacity. It is also prompted by increased use of trade-restrictive measures in other major markets," it added, in reference to the range of tariffs introduced in the US under the Trump administration.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    According to the statement, the import quota covers two types of hybrid vehicle: "full hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), including mild hybrid electric vehicles (MHEVs).".

    Although specifically designed to deal with the influx of Chinese cars into the European market, the country-specific import quota will be valid for all countries whose imports made up more than 2% of EU imports in 2025. Other importers will face a residual cap.

    The goal behind import quotas is to protect a country's, or in this case the European Union's, own producers.

    China has become a major player in the car manufacturing market in recent years, especially when it comes to electric and hybrid vehicles, a sector where European manufacturers have fallen behind.

    It has been revealed that germany, as the EU's largest economy and a major exporter of vehicles, is a primary beneficiary of the import quota. Several of Germany's car manufacturers have announced widespread layoffs as they see their market shares shrink.

    In October, German car manufacturers saw their sales fall by 5.7% in the EU despite a growing market. This meant their market share in the bloc fell from 41.5% to 38.2%, according to consulting firm EY.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    A report by the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) published on Tuesday found that electric vehicles and hybrids have seen a large uptick in latest registrations in Europe in October over the same time last year.

    It found that new electric car registrations were up 61.4% across the bloc while plug-in hybrids were up in particular in Italy (+73.1%), Spain (+32.3%), and Germany (+11%).

    Hybrid electric vehicles were around a third of all latest registrations, with plug-in hybrids making up around 10%.

    "The main beneficiaries of this trend are in China," EY mentioned in comments to AFP. "Chinese manufacturers, which are heavily focused on electric cars and plug-in hybrids, increased their EU sales by 73.4% and achieved a newly introduced record market share of 13.1%.".

    "The market share losses suffered by German manufacturers are not an outlier and are not a problem limited to individual countries — it is a clear trend that is now evident in all major European markets," noted Constantin Gall of EY. "This is alarming, because Europe is the home market of the German auto industry.".

    Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024.
    • A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
    • Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Parastoo Ahmadi's performance was livestreamed on her YouTube channel in December 2024.

    A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.

    Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.

    Recent findings suggest that ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.

    This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.

    In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.

    At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

    There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.

    On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.

    "We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.

    "The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately.".

    Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

    "Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," stated Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

    Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

    In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

    Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

    Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

    In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.

    Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.

    According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.

    Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Dutch Data Protection Authority is urging consumers not to buy AI-enabled camera glasses, warning that they compromise the privacy of nearby bystanders and risk the safety of their people.

    The authority, whose recent statement falls just short of an outright ban, stated that use of the internet-enabled and always-on glasses to record people in public is “almost always prohibited.”.

    According to recent reports, critics have dubbed these smart wearables as “pervert glasses” for their propensity to be used to video people without their permission, particularly to harass women. While some glasses have warning lights when customers are recording, privacy advocates have argued that these alerts are not clear enough. Some people have even made phone apps capable of detecting nearby smart glasses wearers.

    It has been revealed that the Dutch data protection authority warned that the glasses also produce wrong results and unsafe results. In one test carried out by the Dutch authority, a pair of unnamed glasses “gave dating advice to an adult who indicated that they are interested in a minor.” The glasses also incorrectly read a medicine label and claimed to have called an ambulance when it had not.

    The Dutch government’s advice follows a similar move by the Norwegian government, which in September said it was considering a ban on camera-enabled devices.

    #161763. What you can do with your old, discontinued Mac Pro

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (912 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    What you can do with your old, discontinued Mac Pro

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Earlier this year, Apple discontinued its Mac Pro desktop workstation, marking an end to one of the manufacturer's longest-running product lines.
    • Whether you decide to sell your Mac Pro to finance an upgrade to a new Mac Studio, repurpose the existing hardware with a new operating system or simply continue to use the workstation for years to come, you have plenty of options.
    • In a recent development, apple discontinued the Mac Pro in March 2026 in order to prioritize the fresh Mac Studio line of workstations.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mac Pros are becoming obsolete. Do they still have use?

    Earlier this year, Apple discontinued its Mac Pro desktop workstation, marking an end to one of the manufacturer's longest-running product lines. Starting at $5,999 for the entry-level 2019 model and costing tens of thousands of dollars when fully equipped, the Mac Pro was (and still is) a serious investment for most people and companies. Thankfully, even though Apple has stopped making new Mac Pros, your discontinued workstation is hardly worthless.

    Whether you decide to sell your Mac Pro to finance an upgrade to a new Mac Studio, repurpose the existing hardware with a new operating system or simply continue to use the workstation for years to come, you have plenty of options. The secondhand market for Mac Pros remains strong, while the modular nature of the Mac Pro means that running alternative operating systems to keep the device current is easier than it is with newer Mac products. Plus, if it's in working condition, there's nothing stopping you from continuing to use it as intended, even if its hardware is showing its age. Regardless of what you're looking to do, here's everything you need to know about what comes next for your discontinued Mac Pro and how to get the most value out of it.

    In a recent development, apple discontinued the Mac Pro in March 2026 in order to prioritize the fresh Mac Studio line of workstations. With the move to Apple silicon, which uses a highly integrated system-on-a-chip (SoC) design, a modular desktop workstation like the Mac Pro no longer makes sense. Drop-in cards like GPUs aren't compatible with Apple's in-house silicon due to Apple's use of a unified memory architecture for the Apple M-series chips. This architecture shares memory resources across the CPU, GPU and other system components, and there simply isn't a good way to introduce some third-party components commonly used with the 2019 Mac Pro. The 2023 Mac Pro, meanwhile, uses the Apple M2 Ultra SoC and lacks the modularity of the 2019 model, so it's essentially a Mac Studio in a Mac Pro shell.

    Recent findings suggest that apple is also streamlining macOS around its SoC design, something that developers for popular professional software like Adobe Premiere Pro are also doing. Since it would be too cumbersome to develop this kind of sophisticated software for two different kinds of Apple architectures, Apple and its partners are focusing on what's latest rather than trying to continue supporting an increasingly obsolete architecture. Without sufficient software support, it makes little sense to continue producing the Mac Pro.

    While Apple isn't producing fresh Mac Pros, that doesn't mean you have to get rid of yours. Developers are streamlining their apps for Apple M-series Macs, but some app support for Intel-based Macs will likely continue for another couple of years, like security updates and minor fixes. This support will vary between developers, though, and Apple's latest macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn't support the Intel-based Mac Pro.

    Sources indicate that if you have the 2023 Mac Pro, you don't have anything to worry about right now. It will be supported for years to come, and that support includes macOS 27 Golden Gate. Third-party apps will also support the 2023 Mac Pro for as long as they support the Apple M2 Ultra SoC.

    If you're not getting the support you need from macOS on your old Mac Pro, you can install a new OS, either with a virtual machine or through a completely new installation. A guest OS doesn't get rid of macOS, and paid apps like Parallels make installing Ubuntu Linux and Windows 11 relatively painless. There are also free VM options that can help extend your discontinued Mac Pro's life.

    According to recent reports, attempting a full install of a new OS might also be an option, but it's a complicated process and comes with some risk of bricking your Mac Pro for good. There are online resources to walk you through the process, but you'll need some technical know-how, so if you aren't comfortable with that, do not attempt it.

    If you're going to get rid of your old Mac Pro, don't just recycle it — plenty of people will be willing to buy it from you. Many professional workflows, like video editing or running a network server, require a lot of memory but don't necessarily need the fastest processors. Professionals and students in those fields might jump at the chance to pick up a working Mac Pro for relatively cheap. Online marketplaces are good places to start, but a handwritten bulletin board notice at your local university can work just as well.

    If you have a 2019 Mac Pro, its internal components might also be worth selling individually. Memory and large-capacity storage drives are especially in-demand right now, so even though stripping your Mac Pro for parts might feel unseemly, if you can't find a buyer for the whole system, this might be the way to go. Some money is better than nothing.

    It has been revealed that if you plan on getting rid of your Mac Pro, make sure to do a few things beforehand. Read through this support page on Apple's website and follow the instructions for backing up your files, logging out of accounts and performing a factory reset. The last thing you want is to give someone all your sensitive data after saying goodbye to your old Mac Pro for good.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies unveiled Monday.

    CrowdStrike and Zscaler said that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era.

    According to recent reports, zscaler is a San Jose, California-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies. The company offers zero-trust technology, a security feature that requires employees to authenticate each and every time they access an internal system or resource. The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network.

    Recent findings suggest that crowdStrike, which secures the computers, laptops, phones, and other devices connected to a firm’s network, said the deal will unite its endpoint protection software with Zscaler’s zero-trust platform to better defend their customers against data breaches. By combining the two products, CrowdStrike and Zscaler say that they can offer “superior protection” to their customers.

    In remarks on Monday, the companies mentioned that the acquisition will help customers safely adopt AI.

    The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, is expected to close around this time next year.

    Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    • The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo).
    • Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a latest report from the charity Oxfam states, external.
    • Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it notes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo).

    Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a latest report from the charity Oxfam states, external.

    Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it notes.

    Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza "will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival".

    In response, the Israeli embassy in the UK mentioned the report "falls short of professional standards".

    Behar also accused Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza".

    Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. It maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.

    The report says 99% of Gaza indicates indicators of potential environmental contamination.

    Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

    Industry observers note that the report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

    Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.

    "There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.

    She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.

    Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been cleared.

    With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage right now makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.

    In a recent development, testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.

    UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.

    The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It notes special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.

    The Israeli embassy sharply criticised the report, arguing that it relied on satellite imagery "and unverified assumptions, and its methodology lacks the academic rigour needed to withstand serious scrutiny".

    It noted the report drew conclusions about Gaza's soil and groundwater without considering the excavation of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels by Hamas, rendering it fundamentally flawed.

    Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent camps.

    Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.

    A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.

    Industry observers note that "There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he states. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children.".

    Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war.

    Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.

    "Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage.     #161754. Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1145 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Surveillance pricing uses our personal data to make us pay more

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1145 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that “It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense.
    • But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given.
    • In a recent development, surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history, smart devices, and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that “It costs what it costs” is a mindset I’ve found useful when encountering a sizable, but highly necessary or desired, expense. The sentiment encourages me to accept the price because that’s the accepted value of the gadget, app, or service that I really need or want.

    But with surveillance pricing, that comfort is no longer a given. I could end up paying more for my TV because of where I am or more for a software subscription because of my age.

    In a recent development, surveillance pricing leverages data collected from our web history, smart devices, and apps with the goal of getting us to pay more. That obfuscates the value of products, challenges smart shopping and budgets, and makes it harder for people to get products and services at a fair price.

    Surveillance pricing, according to the nonprofit Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC), is an algorithmic pricing practice that charges individuals or groups of individuals different prices “for the same goods or services.”.

    “The goal of surveillance pricing is to infer the highest price that the customer is willing to pay, based on consumers’ personal data and other market data,” EPIC explains.

    Instacart previously practiced surveillance pricing, also called personalized pricing. In 2025, Consumer Reports found that, “based on how much Instacart notes the typical household of four spends on groceries, the average price variations observed could translate into a cost swing of about $1,200 per year.” Instacart has since removed its surveillance pricing tools.

    Dynamic pricing, or surge pricing, differs from surveillance pricing in that, instead of relying on consumer data, it uses changing market trends, like supply and demand, inventory levels, and competitor pricing, to set prices.

    While dynamic pricing may charge you more for an Uber ride when it’s very busy, surveillance pricing can feel less reasonable.

    For instance, Target’s app was previously accused of using location data to charge users $100 more for a TV if they bought it while standing inside a Target store. At the time, Target remarked that it would match lower prices presented by customers, but many customers wouldn’t think to look for pricing discrepancies. In another instance from 2012, Orbitz was found to more prominently feature expensive hotels to people using macOS. Companies often dispute whether their practices truly qualify as surveillance pricing. But these examples all reflect companies using data about their customers to influence the prices they show them.

    ZipRecruiter was one of the first companies to leverage surveillance pricing as we think of it today. In 2018, its profits increased 84 percent by using surveillance pricing versus charging every customer $99. Surveillance pricing is still somewhat nascent, but its potential lucrativeness and the growing availability of user data suggest it may become more common.

    Other technological advancements, including advanced machine-learning methods, have further facilitated the growth of personalized pricing.

    In 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) noted at least 250 companies used surveillance pricing.

    In a recent development, according to a 2025 statement from then-FTC Chair Lina M. Khan, “retailers frequently use people’s personal information to set targeted, tailored prices for goods and services—from a person’s location and demographics, down to their mouse movements on a webpage.”.

    Industry observers note that surveillance pricing has become more widespread as food delivery platforms, rideshare services, rental housing providers, and other businesses have gained access to the technology and data needed to implement it. Third-party data brokers, advertising and analytics companies, and credit providers make it easy for organizations to get the information needed to build customer profiles. The growth of web browsing, the Internet of Things, and user tracking have created data-rich digital lives that are simple for retailers to analyze.

    Additionally, the rise of e-commerce means even more customer data is available, which makes it easier to charge customers different prices than a physical store could.

    Surveillance pricing makes it hard for shoppers to get the best, or even fair, prices and makes it difficult to assess the true value of products. There are also broader implications that go beyond how consumers feel about it.

    A 2025 report from the American Economic Liberties Project, “Prohibiting Surveillance Prices and Wages” (PDF), says surveillance pricing relies on biased algorithms:.

    It has been revealed that algorithms often rely on data that reflect historical and ongoing biases, embedding these prejudices into wage- and price-setting systems and perpetuating them. For example, as studies of rideshare company platforms have shown, riders traveling to predominantly non-white neighborhoods are often charged higher prices,a pattern that mirrors historical residential segregation. And … college test-prep services have sometimes been priced over $1,000 more in zip codes with large Asian populations.

    Dating app Tinder, for example, was previously reported to use surveillance pricing to charge older users more money for subscriptions. Tinder denied that it used social or demographic data for pricing, agreed to pay $60.5 million to settle a class-action lawsuit about the charge, and notes it stopped charging older users more.

    Surveillance pricing also incentivizes data collectors to gather increasingly detailed, potentially intrusive, consumer data, which could be used in harmful or exploitative ways.

    As EPIC states: “Consumers are categorized by data brokers that identify or infer characteristics such as age, demographics, shopping habits, lifestyle, or economic status. Such personal data collected for commercial purposes also often ends up in the hands of third parties, including law enforcement agencies, and is used for unrelated purposes.”.

    Some critics of surveillance pricing argue for legislation that bans the practice or sets parameters about how and when it’s used. However, some argue that legislation could hurt consumers, since surveillance pricing can also show customers lower prices.

    Recent findings suggest that barring legislation, there are things that companies can do to better serve shoppers in this regard. One approach is to disclose when they are using personalized pricing, similar to when Uber alerts users that surge pricing is in effect.

    Speaking of surge pricing, prioritizing dynamic pricing over surveillance pricing would allow organizations to continue leveraging data and real-time market conditions to maximize revenue while reducing the risk of biased or unfair pricing.

    Surveillance pricing often occurs surreptitiously, so consumers, lawmakers, and retailers will likely continue to be challenged by the practice. Consumers can strive to protect themselves somewhat by setting their own standards for what they pay when possible. For instance, when I buy a new TV, I have an idea of how much I am willing or able to spend before I start shopping. If the prices don’t come close to aligning with my needs, I reassess my options, which may include using an aging gadget longer.

    Shoppers should no longer assume that “it costs what it costs.” By setting personal spending limits and deciding in advance what you’re willing to pay, you can avoid paying more for a gadget, app, or service than is fair.

    #161752. Commons reasons your Android phone's icons won't move and how to fix it

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (546 w)

    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Commons reasons your Android phone's icons won't move and how to fix it

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, android phones offer plenty of customization options to help you organize your apps.
    • Many Android phones can auto-arrange icons in your app drawer, usually called automatic sorting.
    • Sources indicate that if your icons aren't moving at all, check your home screen and launcher cache settings.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s most likely your home screen settings.

    According to recent reports, android phones offer plenty of customization options to help you organize your apps. Some settings, unbeknownst to users, can reorganize your phone's icons or prevent you from moving them at all. A home screen that keeps changing can be frustrating, but the good news is you can fix it without much troubleshooting.

    Many Android phones can auto-arrange icons in your app drawer, usually called automatic sorting. This causes your phone to organize icons in alphabetical order, by install date or by other listed criteria. App or OS updates can also change your home screen grid, so don't be alarmed if icons rearrange after a major software patch.

    Sources indicate that if your icons aren't moving at all, check your home screen and launcher cache settings. A locked home screen is the main culprit on most phones. However, if you're using a Google Pixel or stock Android without a locked home screen setting, clearing your launcher cache is another option. Employing either solution is fairly straightforward.

    In a recent development, the most likely cause of locked icons is a locked home screen. Many Android manufacturers enable locked home screens by default, preventing you from moving icons. You can fix this by going into your phone's home screen settings and turning the setting off.

    It has been revealed that most Samsung phones let you access this setting by going to Settings and searching for "Home Screen." From there, look for the option "Lock Home Screen Layout." Toggle it off to enable icon movement again. If you are using another type of Android device, you can usually find this setting under the "Home" tab of your device.

    Industry observers note that once you've unlocked your home screen, you might notice that your icons will sometimes reorganize themselves without your input. This could be due to some auto-sort options in your phone settings. You can find these sorting options in your home screen settings—on Samsung phones, under "Settings," while on some Android phones, under "Home." If your home screen layout is still not to your liking, consider resetting your home screen and restart your phone.

    Sources indicate that on Android devices without a locked home screen layout, such as Google Pixel phones, you may want to clear your launcher cache instead. Your phone's launcher cache saves all temporary data related to your home screen. If this cache gets bloated, it can make your phone more prone to crashing and cause inconsistent home screen behavior, including frozen icons.

    Industry observers note that clearing the launcher cache is similar across Android phones, though the launcher app varies by manufacturer. Head to your phone's settings menu and look through your apps. You're looking for your phone's launcher. Google Pixel uses the Pixel Launcher; Samsung phones use One UI. Select the app and head to its storage settings. You should see an option to clear its cache. After you clear it, you should notice your home screen is more responsive. We also suggest rebooting your phone once you've cleared the cache to ensure it actually gets cleared out. If your phone remains unresponsive, restart your phone in safe mode to see whether a third-party app is causing the problem.

    #161751. Breaking: How the AI trade could trap even cautious investors

    Breaking: How the AI trade could trap even cautious investors

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.
    • After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.
    • The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.

    After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.

    The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

    The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.

    Yet, those seeking a safe haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.

    Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.

    These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.

    Recent findings suggest that most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a company's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.

    The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.

    Sources indicate that the US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Big Tech names.

    The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.

    Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.

    Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.

    According to recent reports, "A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.

    Industry observers note that "That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy.".

    Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," remarked investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.

    Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.

    In MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.

    That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.

    "My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.

    When some investors get over-optimistic about a organization and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.

    Professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.

    "Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small tech giant," remarked Vayanos.

    Industry observers note that the problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral.".

    Recent findings suggest that to cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.

    In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.

    EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage company.

    However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.

    Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.

    Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he told DW, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs.".

    LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks.".

    But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger.".

    In a recent development, A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company.".

    The statement did not identify the tech giant or explain what penalty had been imposed.

    Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]".

    Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.

    Sources indicate that in the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.

    He and the alleged South African pilot are remarked to be the only other survivors.

    South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy".

    "Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.

    In 2022, DR Congo's army blamed M23 rebels, who are now part of the FRN, of shooting down a UN helicopter in which eight people died. The rebels denied it.

    The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.

    In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.

    The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.

    Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.

    Over the weekend, medical charity MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res mentioned fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.

    The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

    The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, A close ally of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump reportedly dialed into an Nvidia board meeting to push for the ousted CEO’s return, Semafor reported on Monday. Trump got his way, as Nvidia unveiled Huang’s reinstatement shortly afterward.

    “I spoke to them, let me put it that way … And I convinced them,” the president told CNBC.

    Huang was forced to step down from his role as CEO, which he held for 33 years, after news broke that he had affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including a direct report.

    According to recent reports, “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor.

    The president took to his social media app, Truth Social, to remark that “the United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security.”.

    According to Nvidia’s press release about Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president, the manufacturer claimed that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

    Industry observers note that while Trump has declared that Huang “did absolutely nothing wrong,” many government officials aren’t buying the president’s point of view. Huang is still expected to testify in closed-door conversations with three committees of the House of Representatives on December 1. He is also slated to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to testify publicly, though that hearing has not been scheduled yet.

    “People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump remarked to CNBC.

    According to recent reports, trump has maintained this position through the scandal, even denying that he was ever told about Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation). The Fresh York Times reported, on the contrary, that Trump’s secretary of state and national security adviser Marco Rubio briefed him aboard Air Force One in May.

    Earlier this spring, Rubio also supervised the drafting of a memo that circulated among top policymakers, warning that Alice Huang was spying for China’s Ministry of State Security.

    #161742. The biggest downsides to using Apple's Magic Mouse

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (729 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    The biggest downsides to using Apple's Magic Mouse

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Apple switched the Magic Mouse to USB-C but left its most questionable design decision untouched, and that isn’t the only thing customers dislike.
    • There are a handful of things that Apple's Magic Mouse does that would make regular mice envious.
    • And it isn't the only reason even committed Mac consumers are calling it quits on the official Apple mouse.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Apple switched the Magic Mouse to USB-C but left its most questionable design decision untouched, and that isn’t the only thing customers dislike.

    There are a handful of things that Apple's Magic Mouse does that would make regular mice envious. The shimmery Multi-Touch surface lets you scroll sideways on a spreadsheet and move across macOS even without that conventional scroll wheel. But then, it is also brilliantly designed to be unusable when the charging cable is plugged in. That's not a small trade-off, especially for a device whose very purpose is to make computer use a breeze.

    And it isn't the only reason even committed Mac consumers are calling it quits on the official Apple mouse. The weirdly slender body looks gorgeous but offers barely any palm space, while the aluminum sides aren't universally loved either. For those who've used a traditional mouse for years, the controls on the Magic Mouse can also feel severely limiting.

    Sources indicate that even after ditching the Lightning port with the 2024 refresh alongside the much faster M4 iMac, Apple decided to leave most of those pain points untouched. Now, in all honesty, the Magic Mouse has a pretty strong fan base, especially among users who love its touch gestures and that classic Apple minimalist design. But if you're spending hours using it, the things it cuts out can matter a lot more than the cool tricks it has.

    It has been revealed that apple unveiled the rechargeable Magic Mouse 2 back in October 2015 with its Lightning port at the bottom. A seemingly controversial design choice even back then, it somehow survived the switch to USB-C almost a decade later. So, every time your Magic Mouse is out of juice, you need to flip it over and leave it be until there's enough power to start using the mouse again.

    Industry observers note that the saving grace here is that the mouse's battery is good for around a month or more between charges, so flipping your Magic Mouse on its back isn't a daily ordeal. But that doesn't make it any less weird, especially since Apple allows its Magic Keyboard and Magic Trackpad to be used while they're plugged in. There's also no clarity from Apple on how many years the rechargeable battery in the Magic Mouse is expected to last.

    Now, let's talk about that shape which puts this slim mouse at just 0.85 inches tall. There's also barely any palm support, and depending on how you're holding it, those aluminum edges can press uncomfortably against your fingers. If you use a fingertip grip, this might be less of a problem, but if you're more of a "resting your entire hand on a mouse" type of person, adjusting your grip is something you'll have to get used to.

    In a recent development, since Apple is asking $79 for the Magic Mouse in white and $99 for the black version, you'd expect the basic functions. While Apple's mouse supports right-clicking with its touch-sensitive surface, there's no middle-click or a programmable thumb button. Using CAD software is where you miss those buttons the most, since holding the middle mouse button is how you usually pan around drawings. Sure, third-party utilities can add some of the missing functionality, but having to install extra software to bring conventional features to a premium mouse is frustrating to say the least.

    You've got to give some credit to the Multi-Touch surface, especially for making scrolling without the usual wheel still feel natural. But do expect accidental swipes like you would on a phone screen since there are no physical controls. Some owners have even faced problems like stuttering and inconsistent tracking. Those could very well be isolated incidents though, and in one case, the lag started right after a macOS update.

    The good part is that Apple doesn't force the Magic Mouse down your throat just because you own a Mac. You can use one of the best wireless mice from other brands on macOS, although you would be missing out on gestures that make the Magic Mouse so special. Logitech's Signature M650, for instance, packs a typical scroll wheel and comes equipped with physical side buttons. Costing about half as much as the Magic Mouse at $39.99, the M650 comes with a contoured grip in place of the Magic Mouse's glossy finish.

    #161739. Russia will launch a routine ISS supply mission tomorrow—apparently, it's a substantial secret

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (777 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Russia will launch a routine ISS supply mission tomorrow—apparently, it's a substantial secret

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It was the most simple of questions.
    • “It’s my understanding there’s another cargo mission going to the ISS this week, a Russian Progress,” Foust said.
    • It has been revealed that this Progress MS-36 cargo launch, mind you, is presently scheduled for fewer than 16 hours from now, at 10:13 UTC (05:13 am ET) on Tuesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It was the most simple of questions. On Monday afternoon, during a NASA news conference about the International Space Station, Space News reporter Jeff Foust asked about an upcoming launch of a Russian spacecraft.

    “It’s my understanding there’s another cargo mission going to the ISS this week, a Russian Progress,” Foust said. “Can you confirm that, and give the date and time that will launch?”.

    It has been revealed that this Progress MS-36 cargo launch, mind you, is presently scheduled for fewer than 16 hours from now, at 10:13 UTC (05:13 am ET) on Tuesday. It is going to a space station co-operated by the US space agency. But no, NASA would not provide this basic information about the upcoming Progress launch.

    “Regarding the Progress launch, I would ask you to please reach out to Roscosmos directly for any questions tied to that vehicle,” stated the senior NASA official on the call, Gaurang Patel, operations integration manager for NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program.

    Industry observers note that effectively, this is a “Go f- yourself” response from NASA. Roscosmos typically does not reply to Western media outlets, and everyone knows this.

    So why is a bog-standard Progress launch suddenly a state secret? It seems to be a recent policy change, because, historically, NASA has televised every one of these cargo flights from Russia’s main spaceport in Baikonur, Kazakhstan. But there is no information about the upcoming launch on NASA’s television schedule for upcoming “live” events.

    As recently as September, NASA provided live television coverage of Progress rolls out from Baikonur. It even issued a media advisory promising to enhancement its broadcast schedule once Roscosmos provided launch details. Two months later, NASA officials apparently are unwilling to confirm that another Progress launch is taking place.

    Sources indicate that the question is whether this decision was made by NASA or was a request from Roscosmos, and, ultimately, whether any of this matters. We can make some educated guesses.

    Sources indicate that it is probably safe to surmise that the decision here was originally made by state-sponsored Russian space corporation Roscosmos. The company has not been advertising the preparation of the Progress spacecraft as it customarily does, some local sources say. Russian space reporter Anatoly Zak confirms that Roscosmos has “dramatically curtailed” its coverage of all launch campaigns in recent months. There is no mention of the launch on Roscosmos’ Telegram channel.

    So why is Roscosmos doing this? There are some novel aspects of this flight. Among the cargo being brought to the space station is a robot that was created to assist spacewalkers during extravehicular activities. Operated by humans, the human-like “Teledroid” is designed to operate in a vacuum, exposed to radiation. Surely nothing will go wrong with this.

    It has been revealed that this is also the first launch of a Progress spacecraft since NASA and Roscosmos agreed that the leaky PrK module on board the space station would be decommissioned. Zak reports that, as a result, the Progress spacecraft will first dock to the Poisk module, where it will be unloaded. It will then be moved from there to the docking port attached to the PrK module to provide propulsion for the space station. Docked there, the ship’s propulsion system is better aligned with the station’s main axis.

    According to recent reports, but none of this likely is the cause of secrecy surrounding Tuesday’s Progress launch. Rather, more likely it is due to Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

    It has been revealed that ars reported earlier this year that, after a spaceport in northern Russia came under attack from drones on multiple occasions, the Russian government put a tighter lid on information about its rolls out from Plesetsk. It now seems likely that Russia has extended this secrecy policy to other missions at other spaceports.

    For example, earlier this month, Russia launched a Soyuz rocket from the Vostochny Cosmodrome without publicly announcing its precise launch date and time beforehand. Roscosmos confirmed the mission only after liftoff, and independent observers had to rely on local government notices to determine when the launch would occur.

    Through all of the geopolitical turmoil on Earth, NASA has sought to maintain a good working relationship with Russia. Most likely, then, NASA has gone along with Russia’s secrecy policy for this week’s cargo launch—absurd though it appears in a culture of transparency.

    Nevertheless, this kind of secrecy would seemingly be untenable with a crewed launch involving NASA astronauts. The next test of this will come in March 2027, when the Soyuz MS-30 mission carrying three astronauts, including NASA’s Deniz Burnham, is due to lift off from Baikonur. We’ll be watching.

    #161735. Jensen Huang isn’t out of the woods yet
